Sluices
SLOO-siz
n. pl. (channels with gates for controlling water; part of Egypt's doomed irrigation economy)
From Old French escluse, from Late Latin exclusa, a floodgate — literally something shut out. In Isaiah it stands in a phrase describing those who make ponds and channels for fish, the artificial waterworks of the Nile delta.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Isaiah 19 is a burden against Egypt, and its most devastating stroke is not military. The waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up. Egypt was the Nile; everything the country had — the flax, the fish, the fowling, the reeds, the annual flood that made the fields — came from one river that had never failed. Isaiah says it will. Then he walks through the economy trade by trade. The fishers shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish; and they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish. The sluice-makers are the engineers, the men whose skill had domesticated the river with gates and channels and stocked ponds. Their purposes break, because the thing they were managing is gone. Egypt is Scripture's standing picture of a civilization that trusts what it can see and control, and Israel's standing temptation was to lean on it: woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and stay on horses, and trust in chariots. The sluices were real engineering and they were excellent, and they could not make it rain.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the stream of water issuing through a floodgate; a vent for water; an opening or channel with a gate.

expand to see more

SLUICE, n. The stream of water issuing through a floodgate; or the floodgate itself; a vent for water.

SLUICE, v.t. To emit by flood gates; to wet abundantly.

POND, n. A body of stagnant water without an outlet, larger than a puddle, and smaller than a lake.

CHANNEL, n. The hollow bed of running waters; a canal or artificial cut for water.

PURPOSE, n. That which a person sets before himself as an object to be reached or accomplished; design; intention.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 19:10 — "And they shall be broken in the purposes thereof, all that make sluices and ponds for fish."

Isaiah 19:5 — "And the waters shall fail from the sea, and the river shall be wasted and dried up."

Isaiah 19:8 — "The fishers also shall mourn, and all they that cast angle into the brooks shall lament, and they that spread nets upon the waters shall languish."

Ecclesiastes 2:6 — "I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees:"

Modern Corruption

Technical mastery is taken as security — a system engineered well enough is thought beyond failure; Isaiah breaks the sluice-makers' purposes by drying the river their whole craft presupposed.

expand to see more

Egypt's engineers were not fools and Isaiah does not call them fools. Their sluices worked. What the prophecy exposes is the hidden assumption underneath every such system: that the supply will continue. Modern equivalents are easy to name and painful to examine — supply chains, grids, credit, the assumption that food appears in shops. Scripture's quarrel is not with skill or with planning; Joseph stored grain for seven years by the wisdom of God, and Proverbs praises the ant that provideth her meat in the summer. It is with the confidence that competent arrangements have removed our dependence on God, when in fact they have only made it harder to notice.

Solomon ran the experiment from the inside and wrote it down. I made me pools of water, to water therewith the wood that bringeth forth trees — along with houses, vineyards, gardens, orchards, servants, silver and gold, and every delight he could name. His verdict on the whole works was vanity and vexation of spirit. Not because the pools were wrong, but because they could not do what he had half-hoped they would. The remedy is not to build worse but to hold what we build the way James instructs: ye ought to say, if the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew seker (H7938), a dam or enclosure of water; yeor (H2975), the Nile; agam (H98), a pool or marsh; charash (H2796), a craftsman.

expand to see more

Hebrew seker (H7938) — a dammed enclosure; rendered sluices, used once in Scripture.

Hebrew yeor (H2975) — the Nile, the river; the whole subject of Isaiah's burden against Egypt.

Hebrew agam (H98) — a pool or reedy marsh; the ponds for fish.

Hebrew amal (H535) — to languish, to be feeble; the fate of the fishermen and the flax workers alike.

Hebrew hevel (H1892) — vapour, vanity; Solomon's verdict on his own pools and orchards.

Usage

"“they shall be broken in the purposes thereof” — the engineers' plans, not their skill, undone."

"“the river shall be wasted and dried up” — the assumption beneath the whole craft removed."

"“I made me pools of water” — Solomon running the experiment and recording the verdict."
